title: Does God Have a Plan for My Life?
excerpt: Jeremiah 29:11, Romans 8:28 and Proverbs 3:5-6 are read in their settings, where each says something harder than the greeting card. Scripture says plainly that God governs; whether he has a route for each life that must be found is argued among Christians, and no wrong turn puts a person outside his care.
body:
A young woman has two job offers in two cities and has been praying for three weeks for some sign of which one God wants. A woman of fifty, whose marriage ended last year, was told at twenty that God had a wonderful plan for her life, and she lies awake going back over the forks in the road to find the one where she left it. A man standing at a graveside was handed a card with a verse on it about plans for welfare and a future and a hope. He read it twice and put it in his pocket, and he hasn't decided what he thinks of the person who gave it to him.

The skeptic thinks the whole idea is a comfort that can't be tested. When things go well the believer says it was the plan, and when they go badly he says it was the plan too, and mysterious. An explanation that fits every outcome, he says, explains nothing. It is a way of feeling watched over in a universe that isn't watching.

He is right about one use of the phrase. "It was God's plan" tells nobody why a thing happened, and Christians should stop offering it as though it did. What the Bible says on the subject is more careful than the greeting cards. It also turns out that the title holds two questions. One is whether God governs a person's life. The other is whether God has a blueprint for that life which the person is supposed to find and follow. Scripture answers the first plainly, and Christians disagree about the second.

## Three Verses

Three sentences carry most of the weight in popular talk about God's plan, and each of them means something a little different when it is read where it stands.

The first is from Jeremiah. "For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope" (Jeremiah 29:11). It comes from a letter the prophet sent to the Jews who had been deported to Babylon. The Study Bible's note on [Jeremiah 29](/study/bible/jeremiah/29) points out that every "you" in the promise is plural. God is speaking to a people. The sentence just before it sets the schedule: "When seventy years are completed for Babylon, I will visit you" (Jeremiah 29:10). Most of the adults who first heard that letter read aloud would die in Babylon. A rival prophet had been promising that the exile would be over "within two years" (Jeremiah 28:3), and Jeremiah's letter was written partly to call that a lie. In the meantime the exiles were told to "build houses and live in them; plant gardens and eat their produce" and to "seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile" (Jeremiah 29:5, 7).

So the promise is real, and it is harder than it sounds. It tells a defeated people that God has not finished with them and that their grandchildren will go home. It does not tell any one of them that this year will go well. It was written against the prophet who promised quick relief.

The second is Paul's. "And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose" (Romans 8:28). The chapter around it is about suffering. A few lines earlier Paul speaks of "the sufferings of this present time" (Romans 8:18), and a few lines later he lists what he has in mind: "tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword" (Romans 8:35). The good he means is defined in the next verse, where those God has called are "to be conformed to the image of his Son" (Romans 8:29). The Study Bible's note on the chapter puts it this way: "Paul doesn't call those things good. He says they cannot defeat God's purpose." The verse promises that nothing will be wasted in the end. It does not say why any particular thing happened, and it was never meant to be handed to a grieving person as an explanation.

The third is from Proverbs. "Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make straight your paths" (Proverbs 3:5-6). This is often read as a method for decisions: stop reasoning, wait, and God will show the route. But in Proverbs a straight path is a moral description. Its opposite is the path of those "whose paths are crooked, and who are devious in their ways" (Proverbs 2:15), and the verse that follows the famous two says what the trust consists of: "Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the Lord, and turn away from evil" (Proverbs 3:7). The promise is that a life that fears God will run true. It is not a promise about which city to move to, and it does not ask anyone to stop thinking. The whole book is an appeal to get wisdom.

## What Scripture Means by God's Will

The Bible uses the phrase "the will of God" in two ways, and a good deal of confusion comes from running them together.

Sometimes it means what God has decided shall happen. Paul speaks of the one "who works all things according to the counsel of his will" (Ephesians 1:11). James tells merchants making their plans for the year, "you ought to say, 'If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that'" (James 4:15). This will is certain, and for the most part it is not disclosed ahead of time. Moses said so: "The secret things belong to the Lord our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law" (Deuteronomy 29:29).

At other times the phrase means what God wants from people, and this will is public. "For this is the will of God, your sanctification" (1 Thessalonians 4:3). "Give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you" (1 Thessalonians 5:18). "He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the Lord require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?" (Micah 6:8).

It is worth noticing which of the two the New Testament tells believers to find out. When Paul writes, "do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is" (Ephesians 5:17), he is in the middle of a passage about how to live, and he goes on to speak of drunkenness, singing, marriage and work. It is hard to find a passage that instructs a Christian to discover in advance the first kind of will, the secret one, for his own life.

On the first of the title's two questions, then, the church has spoken with one voice. God governs. The Heidelberg Catechism of 1563 says that all things, "leaf and blade, rain and drought, fruitful and barren years, food and drink, health and sickness, riches and poverty," come "not by chance but by His fatherly hand." Jesus said that not a sparrow falls "apart from your Father" (Matthew 10:29). Christians differ about how God's rule and human freedom fit together, and the essay on [whether God chose who would be saved](/writing/did-god-choose-who-would-be-saved) sets out those accounts. All of them confess a Father who rules. None of them confesses fate.

## Three Views of Guidance

The second question, whether God has a particular route for each person and expects it to be found, has three main answers among Christians who all take Scripture seriously. The site's page for someone facing a decision, [How do I know what God wants me to do?](/help/decisions), says that the creeds do not settle it, and this essay doesn't either.

The first answer is that God has a specific will for each life, covering the large choices of work, marriage and place, and that he makes it known to those who seek it through Scripture, prayer, counsel, circumstances and inward conviction. Its holders point to a psalm, "in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me" (Psalm 139:16), and to Paul's sentence about "good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them" (Ephesians 2:10). They point to the stories: Abraham called out of his country, the church at Antioch told to "set apart for me Barnabas and Saul" (Acts 13:2), Paul turned away from two provinces and summoned to a third by a vision in the night (Acts 16:6-10). The strength of this view is that it takes God's care for particulars at full value. What it fears is a Christianity in which God is consulted about morals and ignored about everything else. Its hard question is that the stories it cites concern turning points in the mission of the apostles, and that no letter of the New Testament tells ordinary believers to look for such a will or explains how. It also has to answer the woman who lies awake. If there was one right road, what becomes of the person who took another?

The second answer is that God's will for a believer is what he has revealed, and that inside those limits a Christian is free, and required, to choose wisely. Its holders point out how the apostles actually made decisions. Paul tells a widow that "she is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord" (1 Corinthians 7:39). He explains his travel plans by giving reasons: "I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, for a wide door for effective work has opened to me" (1 Corinthians 16:8-9). The council in Jerusalem announced its decision with the words "it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us" (Acts 15:28). On this view a believer prays for wisdom, which God promises "generously to all without reproach" (James 1:5), takes advice, since "without counsel plans fail" (Proverbs 15:22), decides, and trusts God with the result. Its comfort, as the site's page on [purpose](/help/purpose) states it, is that "you can't miss God's will by choosing between two good things." What it fears is superstition, and the sentence "God told me" used to end an argument. Its hard question is whether it leaves God too far off. In the book of Acts the Spirit does more than supply principles. He forbids a road and opens another.

The third answer puts the weight on the present leading of the Spirit. God still speaks to his people, by an impression in prayer, a word from another believer, a passage that will not let go, and a Christian should expect it and learn to recognize it. "For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God" (Romans 8:14). The church's history has stories of this kind. Augustine tells in his *Confessions* how, weeping in a garden over a life he could not change, he heard a child's voice from a nearby house chanting, "Take up and read; take up and read." He took it, he says, as "a command to me from Heaven," opened the book of the apostles he had left lying nearby, read "that paragraph on which my eyes first fell," and found his doubt gone. The strength of this view is that it expects a living God. What it fears is a church that believes in the Spirit on paper and would be alarmed if he did anything. Its hard question is how to tell the Spirit's voice from one's own. Paul's sentence about being led stands in a passage about putting sin to death, not about choosing between roads. And Acts itself shows the difficulty. At Tyre the disciples, "through the Spirit," told Paul not to go on to Jerusalem (Acts 21:4). He went, and his friends finally said, "Let the will of the Lord be done" (Acts 21:14). Even the first Christians had to interpret what they were given, and they did not always agree. The page on decisions offers a test that all three views accept: "an impression that contradicts Scripture isn't from him, however strong it feels."

These answers overlap more than their defenders sometimes admit. The same page says that the first two "lead to much the same practice: pray, search the Scriptures, seek counsel, choose, and trust him."

## The Fear of Missing It

The fear deserves more care than the theory. Many Christians carry a picture of God's plan as a single track laid down in advance, with their own life as a train that left it at some forgotten junction years ago. Everything since, on that picture, has been second best.

Scripture has no such picture. Its people take wrong roads constantly, and the purpose of God is not shown waiting for them back at the junction. Joseph's brothers sold him out of hatred, and he told them long afterward, "you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good" (Genesis 50:20). Jonah took a ship in the opposite direction, and "the word of the Lord came to Jonah the second time" (Jonah 3:1). Peter denied his Lord three times beside a fire and was given the church to feed. If the first view of guidance is right and God has a particular will for each life, then the God who has it is also able to bring his people into it. A plan that one mistake could ruin would depend on the person and not on God. The help page says it in a sentence: "Scripture never tells a believer that one wrong turn has put them beyond God's reach."

That has to be said without pretending choices cost nothing. Some doors don't reopen. A marriage that has ended has ended, and years are not handed back. The psalm does not say the faithful never stumble. It says, "though he fall, he shall not be cast headlong, for the Lord upholds his hand" (Psalm 37:24). To the woman of fifty the Bible does not say that nothing was lost. It says she is not living outside the care of God, because nobody can get there by a wrong turn.

To the young woman with two offers the same page gives advice that all three views can accept. Write the decision down in one sentence, pray it plainly, and then, it says, "It doesn't have to be settled by morning." A psalm adds a rebuke to the wish for a sign: "Be not like a horse or a mule, without understanding, which must be curbed with bit and bridle" (Psalm 32:9). God, it seems, would sooner have a daughter who thinks than an animal that is steered.

## What the Plan Does Not Promise

We have made promises with this doctrine that the text does not make. We printed a sentence written to exiles, about a rescue seventy years off, on graduation cards, and let the graduates assume it meant a good job. We told people in hospital corridors that everything happens for a reason, as if we knew the reason. The site's study of providence names the habit of reading God's rule "as a code that can be deciphered," so that every tragedy becomes a message, and it calls that the error of Job's friends. We have committed it often, mostly out of a wish to say something.

Whatever plan God has for a Christian, the New Testament describes its goal as likeness to Christ, and Christ's own road went through a garden where he prayed, "not my will, but yours, be done" (Luke 22:42). Paul traveled to Jerusalem "constrained by the Spirit, not knowing what will happen to me there, except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and afflictions await me" (Acts 20:22-23). That was the plan of God for an apostle. It is a serious thing to tell a twenty-year-old that God has a wonderful plan for her life without telling her what the word wonderful has sometimes covered.

Nothing in this essay explains the grave the man was standing beside. Scripture gives him no reason for it. It tells him who holds him, and it lets him say whatever he needs to say to God in the meantime. [Find Help](/help) has a page for grief and people who can be called.

After the resurrection Jesus told Peter something of how Peter's life would end, and it was not good news. Peter turned, saw another disciple following, and asked what would happen to him. Jesus answered, "If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!" (John 21:22). Peter was given a person to follow. He was not shown the route, his own or anyone else's. The young woman still has to choose a city by Friday.

*"The secret things belong to the Lord our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever."* (Deuteronomy 29:29)

*"The heart of man plans his way, but the Lord establishes his steps."* (Proverbs 16:9)
